subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
Therefore, it
appears to me that neither according to legal interpretation, nor in a common sense point of view, is there anything to be said in favour of the proposition of my right hon. friend. If that Militia Act was framed for anything, it was framed for the defence of Canada. The framers of that Act saw beyond the conditions of that day, and placed within its sections the provision that the militia could be used in or out of Canada, on any invasion or any threat of an invasion, and, therefore, it was made wide enough to include the action which Canada has taken. lAnd, in these three years of war, my right hon. friend has seen that action and he has not protested against it. He.has only felt, it .seems, that, at this particular moment of crisis, it is his duty now to question the Act, and its powers, and to present a new and dilatory solution of the difficulty.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition took up the pledge said to have been given by my right hon. friend the leader of the Government, and, at this late day, he challenges the course Parliament and the Government have taken in respect to the pledge of 500,000 men. It is within the fair knowledge of all in Parliament, and out of Parliament, that this war has been one of the most unexpected developments that the w6rld has ever seen. No man skilled in strategy and military experience, no nation or empire, however far back its warlike prowess and warlike traditions might extend, and no nation or leaders of a nation anywhere, but have been absolutely surprised at the new and fresh develop-

ments which have taken place in this war. There is no need in an intelligent body like this to labour that argument for a single moment. Everybody has been surprised, and everybody has had to make change of methods and of ideas. Was there a nation more deeply embedded constitutionally, in experience, in traditions of the theory of the defence of Empire, even to strong and widely distributed offensive operations, by virtue of enlistment, and voluntary enlistment at that-than the Mother Empire of which we form a part? When that war commenced there were few men in Britain, statesmen or soldiers, who did not believe the contest could be fought and victory won on the old voluntary principle of the enlistment of British people for the defence of their country. War was commenced with that thoroughly embedded in their minds, and embedded in the practices and methods by which they sought to carry on the war. But experience is the mightiest teacher of all, and before necessity the most stubborn of inherited beliefs must give way, and the time came when Great Britain's statesmen, military men, business men, and working people as well, dame to the conclusion that, if Britain was to be saved and the war was to be won, something other than voluntary enlistment must be appealed to, and applied, and it has been appealed to and it has been applied, and millions and millions of men from those little islands in the North sea have cheerfully submitted to compulsion, changed their beliefs and their methods, and did so because it was necessary for the defence of their country, and the victorious outcome of the war.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
And in Canada as well we had known nothing of compulsory enlistment. Ours had been the militia system, which is a voluntary system. We started in the beginning of this war with all our fervour, zeal, and devotion to principle, on the line of voluntary enlistment. We thought that would suffice, and if the war had lasted no longer than it was generally supposed at its commencement that it would last, voluntary enlistment would have carried us over the war, and would have brought us to victory. But it did not so pan out. The war did not end in six, twelve, twenty-four, nor thirty-four months. It is still continuing, and the principle of voluntary enlistment, if it was ever thoroughly tested m a country with

confidence that it would do the work was .so tested in Canada, and it has failed. It did not meet the continued stress of the war and the continued call for men. At the commencemeiit of the war we adopted the voluntary system, in the belief that that system would be sufficient. We proceeded upon that line of action; we expected to continue it; we expected by it to gain the victory and to achieve the result for which we were striving. Proceeding upon that line of action, we sent forward 300,000 or 400,000 of the citizens of Canada. They marched towards the trenches; they went with our plaudits, our good will and our prayers. Not one of them left these shores with the least doubt in his heart that the people of Canada would stand behind the work to which he was devoting himself. My right hon. friend makes much of suggested cleavages, of possible dissensions, and of adherence to constitutional principles. But is there not an implied contract in the great deed of consecration of 400,000 of our men, who, putting their lives in the balance, went out with our plaudits-to do what? Flash a temporary spark of heroism into the atmosphere of the world, which would reflect credit upon Canada? No ! This they were willing to do; this, indeed, they did. But they went forth to win a great world and Empire fight. That is what they went forth to do; that was our contract with them. Shall we make it good, so that as they fall something effective shall be done to guarantee that their heroic sacrifice shall not have been in vain and that the purpose for which they went forward shall be accomplished? That is my way of looking at it; is that not an eminently practical, a moral, and a fair way of looking at it? At this moment the men at the front look back and listen for the footsteps of comrades marching to the front to help them and to take on the work when their arm fails. Is there not in that all the sanctity of a contract which we must fulfil? And ought not that implied contract to count against little differences and little dissensions that may be caused here if.,we take the only step that will bring victory and that will achieve the results for the attainment of which we passed on all this precious and priceless material of manhood as of full weight and put it into the balance?
So, after nearly three years of trial, voluntary enlistment fell down, but not until it had been fully tried. In no country in the world was there a. better class o.f men and women than those who throughout the

major .part of Canada traversed every settlement, every town and every hamlet, and, by all kinds of appeal and encouragement, called for volunteers. There was the finest co-operation amongst the civilians of Canada, and it told mightily in the enlistments that took place. But the inevitable happened, and at last there came the dreary months when fresh enlistments were scarcely more than sufficient to make up the wastage among those troops in Canada who had enlisted for overseas service, but who were gradually subjected to weeding out. That went on from week to 'week and from [DOT] month to month until those earnest souls who had in countless numbers spent their energies, their time and their money in attempting to bring about enlistment, came to us in one great body and said: we can do no more; we can go no further. Was that the experience in Canada, or was it not? It is open to us to answer that question for ourselves.
Then, Sir, still wishing to make full trial of the principle of voluntary enlistment, we designed a force of 50,000 men for home defence. It was honestly designed, 1^ may tell my right hon. friend-although he casts some disparagement upon its motive. My right hon. friend must remember that some 50,000 men who had .enlisted for overseas were kept here in Canada for purposes of guard and for home duty. The enlistment of 50,000 men for home defence would have liberated those 50,000 men who had been kept here for purposes of home defence. There was common sense; there was possibility of aid, in that arrangement. It was tried honestly and to the uttermost, and, for one cause or another, it absolutely failed.
Then the Prime Minister spent some weeks in England. He was at the very centre of the forces; he saw the very inner core of the conditions; he became acquainted with the precise nature of the situation at the front and with the matters reviewed in the councils of war in Great Britain and France. As Pirime Minister he has, from the time war broke out, uttered no backward word; taken no retrogressive step. He has in season and out of season pressed the issues of this great conflict upon the people of Canada and unselfishly devoted [DOT]his time and his energy to the great duty of carrying on the war. He came back from the front convinced that the necessities of the case, the peril of the occasion, made it absolutely necessary that our men should be sustained^ Adding that conviction to the knowledge gained when he came home, he arrived at the conclusion -and we arrived at the same conclusion- that more would have to be done than could be done by relying upon voluntary enlistment.	'
And this measure is the explanation and the interpretation of the conclusions to which he and we arrived, and it is now before the House and the country. Because the Prime-Minister, working along the lines which I have briefly indicated, wished to avoid compulsion or selective conscription, whichever you may call it as long as possible, and desired to work on the old voluntary lines, whilst they seemed possible of success, is it to be urged that he failed in duty if, in order not to injure to the least possible degree the fulness of the work that might be accomplished under the voluntary system, he had uttered no discouraging word? But at last he had to come to the conclusion that if the war was to be won he must pass over - from the ground of voluntary enlistment and ask for a reasonable and intelligent application of the principle of selective service, and he is now here with that conclusion, forced upon him by the necessities of the case and the experience of three years of war.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, when we face such conditions as that, chops logic and talks of the Constitution. Logic is good in its place and constitutions are most excellent, but neither logic nor the Constitution is superior to the people, and they cannot be allowed to be a bar to the people's necessary defence and ultimate salvation. Constitutions are methods through which government of the people is carried on by themselves, in an orderly and methodical way. But the good of the people, the happiness of the people, the salvation of the people, are the basic things which are to be sought after, and just at this very moment it seems to me that in Canadavin the Empire, and throughout the world, we have a situation surrounded with conditions altogether unusual in the history of the world, and which demand action of the real strong red-blooded type for the support of the men we have sent to the front, and for the salvation of the country for which they have gone. My right hon. friend may talk about the Constitution and urge his points in a logical way, but that does not satisfy me. If necessity is upon us, we must act.
I will put this case to my right hon. friend. Suppose that what he hinted at as

have rivalled each other in peace; they have proved doughty assailants in vrar and they have proved strong and firm friends in peace. These men live in this country and we live in this country and the Dominion belongs to us both. Pity it is, pity it will ever remain, if because of this fight for freedom and high ideals and for the liberty and defence of our common country, we do not march more closely side by side with each other so that in the future we may walk more closely side by side when the war is over and the victory won, the country safe, and we are left to our long generations and centuries of mutual toil for progress and advancement in this country. No one hates dissension on this line more than I do. No one could wish more deeply than I do that we saw more eye to eye in this particular matter.
But, the French Canadian is a law-abiding citizen and if he is convinced that this war, to be won, must be won by throwing men into the contest more and more than we have; if the Parliament of Canada comes to that conclusion, and the people that is behind it arrives at that conclusion towards this measure, no one can convince me that the French Canadian will not walk side by side with his fellows in obedience to the law and in perfect unanimity therewith.
I have to speak now with complete frankness and without any other thought than to come to the right and the truth of the matter, and I put a question to my right hon. friend. In all these three years of the war, the French-Canadian has had less opportunity for learning the rights of this great cause and of this great contest, whether from his occupation and his rural habits of thought he is less in the sphere of information and of knowledge. I have just one thing to say, and it is that I believe that things would not be as they are to-day if my right hon. friend and his able, loyal and enthusiastic French followers had done something more than they have done to enlighten the masses of the people in Quebec., with reference to the paramount issues of this war. The words gripped my heart and made me optimistic when my right hon. friend said on one occasion: "No danger from Germany, none, her policy is to be a friend of this country, but if she ever does show her teeth, if sh6 ever does come in opposition to this country with her fleet or her army, then I will go down into the province of Quebec, and I will stump that province from one end to the other in order
TSir (leorge Foster.!
to rouse the people to the defence of the country." For three years this sanguinary war has been going on. I do not want to attempt to admonish or teach other people their duty; I simply state frankly that I deplore the fact that further means of educating the French people on the vital, paramount issues of this war, have not been put in operation in Quebec by its representative men. Whether it is the fault of Sir Sam Hughes, of Sir Edward Kemp, the English people or the French leaders themselves it is deplorable that more has not been done in that direction. If more had been done in that direction, we have the authority that was quoted this afternoon by my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that the French people would have risen en masse in favour of this war.
Now, putting all these things together, I come to the end of my remarks with one final reference to the referendum. It may be the practice of democracy. It has been occasionally the practice of statesmen in Canada, when subjects difficult of solution arose, that they did not wish to give a lead upon, to refer these subjects by referendum to the people, and do nothing thereafter, but the referendum moved on the second reading of this Bill, at this particular time in the crisis which is upon us is, to my mind, a miserable dilatory motion, and nothing else.
* Some hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
With our men in the very front trenches, for members of Parliament and of the Government to down tools in the face of the trenches and enter upon a two or three months' excursion throughout the Dominion of Canada on the idle wind of a referendum, which would settle nothing, but would set us back four months or more, would be little short of criminal. We still would have to make laws, assume responsibilities and carry on in the best interests of Canada, referendum or no referendum. I can see some merit in an appeal to the country on a settled policy, either from this Government or from a coalition government such as was offered to my hon, friend a few days ago.
I can see some finality to that, but to a referendum, none. -It is a dilatory motion, pure and simple. It can result in nothing, but months of turmoil and bitterness at home and delay and confusion and loss abroad whilst the Hun wears down our sons and kinsmen at the front who call to us in vain for help. But I am not very much afraid on that score, because my faith is

constant that this House and Parliament will not give its assent to such a method of avoiding our responsibilities and shelving, for months the war and the most important question that the war has imposed upon us.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was struck, as I am sure the House was intended to be struck, by the suggestion in the first sentences of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), that the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) did not know there was a war in progress. This Bill was brought before the House on its second reading, by the Prime Minister of Canada, without reference to its provisions, to its scope, to its possibilities; a Bill that, if it means anything, means the taking of son from mother, of husband from wife, of father from children, from one end of this Dominion to the other-and it is not worthy a word of explanation by the Prime Minister of Canada when he brings it before the House for its second reading. Does the Government of Canada know the meaning and effect of this measure that it is bringing before the House? Does it know that Canada is at war? We are in a world crisis, the greatest crisis in history. Canada is a participant in that crisis, and the first lieutenant of the Prime Minister, in addressing the Parliament of Canada, through all his rounded periods, through all his well-turned sentences, preserved an air of detachment as though the Government of Canada of which he is a member had no responsibility for the direction of Canada's affairs in this war. We are dealing with a measure for the conscription of men, of one hundred thousand men, to take part in this war, and this measure of conscription is passed over as lightly as though it meant nothing. If it is adopted, it must be adopted, because voluntary enlistment in this country has broken down in Canada. And why has voluntary enlistment broken down? Who is responsible for the breaking down of voluntary enlistment?

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
Who is the Government of Canada, responsible ^for the direction of its affairs? If we are to-day faced with the
necessity of this measure, a measure terrible in its character and in its consequences, my hon. friend and his colleagues would do well to take a few minutes of the time of the House and of the country to explain why that measure is necessary, because under, their administration voluntary enlistment has broken down.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) spoke in eloquent terms, in moving terms, of the responsibilities resting on the people of this country, responsibilities to the men who have gone to carry our name with honour at the battlefront. He said, we were to support them, to see that the sacrifices they made were not in vain; their sacrifice was to be recognized by others and still others and still others of our citizens, so that the honour of Canada would still and always be maintained, not by conscription, but by voluntary service, a service that would do honour to Canada and do credit to the Empire. I say the question is up to the members of the Government to-day to tell this country why it is now, at this stage, necessary to resort to this measure of conscription. The country that has sent 350,000 men to the battle front in voluntary service, is that country lacking in enthusiasm for the cause of the Allies? Surely the country that sends 350,000 can send a few more, could send a few more, would send a few more, if the enthusiasm that has been exhibited in the past had received proper direction and encouragement at the hands of this Government, of which my hon. friend is such an eloquent member. Is there no responsibility resting upon him and upon them? If that river of men has ceased to flow, what strange thing has occurred in Canada that, at the end of April, 1917, this river was still flowing, there was no question that it would continue to flow, and in June, 1917, there is no further flow of voluntary enlistment to be expected, if the honour of Canada is to be maintained it must be maintained by compulsory and not by voluntary service? The honour of the people of Canada in their support of the Allies in this war is discredited by my hon. friend in his remarks to-day, as by the measure that is before the House in whose support those remarks were made. There is some responsibility somewhere in this country of Canada, and it rests upon the Government of Canada, in regard to the direction of our affairs. Has there been honest endeavour,

~ COMMONS
has there been persistent and honest endeavour, to maintain the honour of Canada by voluntary enlistment during the three years that have passed? I do not wish to delay the House seriously, but that is a point that should be settled, and I am fortunate in being able to produce the reports of Hansard to show what direction the efforts of the Government took. Sir Sam Hughes, speaking on January 30, 1917, said:
But here another hindrance stepped in. I do not know whether it was in the interest of munition workers or not.
I think he meant munition " makers He continued: t
But I stand here to say that I look on all this talk of munition workers as piffle, compared with the need of men at the front, piffle of the worst kind-this kind of piffle of considering men getting $7 a day in munition works as compared with a man in the trenches, running the risk of being blown to pieces. It is piffle, and the commonest sort of piffle.
An order in council was passed forbidding the Department of Militia from authorizing a battalion here, there or elsewhere, and it is said that the reason was that too many battalions were being raised in Toronto, Winnipeg, Montreal and other large cities.
Continuing, he said:
The point is that they said:	Here, you
must not have so many regiments recruiting in Toronto or so many recruiting in Montreal.
Sir Robert Borden:	I think what my hon.
friend says might be misunderstood. There was not an order in council passed saying that no further battalions should be recruited, but that no further battalions should be recruited without an order in council.

I have heard, all sorts of stories, but I have never asked my officers. When I came back my officers made certain statements ; they had been directed to go slow in recruiting, but I never asked; I do not know whether it is true or not.
However, seeing the falling off, seeing the need of straining every nerve we could strain at the front, when I came back I set to work to try and get the pulse of the boys. I have always been in favour of universal service, training the boys. I did not deem conscription necessary, and it was not. I could have raised 500,000 men by voluntary enlistment. I could have raised 600,000 by voluntary enlistment without any trouble, I believe. That is only a statement; but I believe I could have done it. However, this order in council stopping the authorization of regiments was

passed, and the talk came on from every hand I presume paid for by German agents- against taking men from munition works.
Speaking on February 1, Sir Robert Borden said:
The fact that we succeeded in the first three and a half months of the past year in recruiting a hundred thousand men or more is an indication that the work was carried on with a good deal of vigour and with a great deal of success. The criticism has been made that proper regard to selection was not made. I discussed that question with the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence more than a year ago- I think in the autumn of 1915 for the first time. The course which my colleague took in that regard was that he did not think at that time that any more systematic method was necessary, and he said that it would be possible, through instructions given to his recruiting officers, to prevent unwise selection, selection which might result in the closing up of industries essential for the prosecution of the war, - when recruits might have been obtained from other classes whose work and service were not so essential. I was informed by General Hughes that instructions had been given in various instances to adopt methods which would give some system to that purpose.
Mr. Oliver:	About what time was that?
Sir Robert Borden:	I think it was in the
autumn of 1915 or early in 1916.
Sir Sam Hughes:	Early in 1916.
Sir Robert Borden:	Early in 1916, I think,
and afterwards it was thought better that the purpose could be carried out in connection with other objects in a more comprehensive way by the proposals for National Service, and that is the explanation of the course which was taken.
So that we have it on the authority ,of the ex-Minister of Militia that so early as the fall of 1915 or early in 1916 a deliberate policy of retarding of recruiting was entered upon as between the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia. At whose instigation? At the demand of the fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters or children of the men who were volunteering to go to the front to carry the flag of Britain and uphold the honour of Canada? No; at the instigation of the munition makers, the munition profiteers who are fattening upon the blood of their country and who, through the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, denied to their employees the privilege of going to the front to fight the battles of the Empire and uphold the honour of Canada.

As to the position taken by a member of the Government on the floor of this House -and the idea was carried through the whole of the Government service, as far as the Government could reach-that there was not as great necessity for the services of able-bodied men at the front as there was in other places, I ask that member of the Government why my son or another man's son should go in the place of his secretary? Our sons are just as good to us as my hon. friend's private secretary was to him.
Having reached the point where the munitions makers of Canada have the sanction of the Premier and of the Minister of Militia in preventing the recruiting of their employees or near-employees, it does not
154J
come with good grace from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, eloquent though he may be, to declare on the floor of Parliament that Canada is not able to make good any promise she has made in the matter of voluntary enlistment. Let those who first made the promise and who later stood in the way of its fulfilment take the responsibility.
My hon. friend suggested that the leader of the Opposition by his proposal of a referendum was standing in the way of efficient and timely prosecution of the war on the part of Canada; I think that was the impression he desired to convey. The leader of the Opposition is the leader of the Opposition. It is his business to bring to the attention of the country sueh direction of its affairs as appears to be best in his judgment. It is the business of the Government to direct those affairs, and if it is true, and it is true, that voluntary enlistment has shown a decrease since the middle of last year, I ask my hon. friend *what he and his colleagues have been doing between then and now to protect the interests of this country should there be a German invasion? It was known in June of last year that there was no prospect under the conditions then prevailing of the promise of the Prime Minister being fulfilled, that the rate of enlistment was such that there was no likelihood of the complement of the 500,000 men being raised within any reasonable time. What was the course of the Government under those circumstances? There was plenty of time between then and now to have taken a referendum, plenty of time for the Germans to have invaded and over-run Canada. They appointed my good friend from Calgary as Director of National Service, and sent postal cards presumably to everybody in the Dominion. That was their idea of how to deal with the question when the Hun was at the gates. They got some of those postal cards back, and the Director of National Service is still the Director of National Service. But there is no Service, individual or national, so "far as any one can judge. This Government spent its time month after month, and month after month practically walking around in a circle, deluding its friends who were in favour of more drastic action into the belief that National Service meant conscription and at the same time giving Dorchester and other places in that neighbourhood clearly to understand that National Service did not mean conscription.

speechtext:
If the conditions are in any degree as my hon. friend declared them to be, what answer has this Government to make to the fact that for one whole year they knew of those conditions and did nothing to remedy them? They did worBe than nothing. When the announcement of National Service was made the effect was necessarily to injure still further voluntary enlistment. When it was announced that the Government was going to take upon itself the responsibility of deciding whether this or that man should go to the front and this or that man into a munitions factory, the responsibility of choosing between the man who was to get $1.10 a day with the privilege of getting shot, and the man who would earn $5 a day in a munitions factory and live in comfort, what young man, unless he was inspired by enthusiasm in more than the ordinary degree, would not naturally say, "The Government is taking the responsibility off my shoulders. It is no longer for me but for the Government to decide whether I shall go to the front or into a munitions factory." I ask you, Sir, whether that was a stimulus to recruiting? When that announcement had gone abroad and recruiting still further fell off, the 'Government did nothing more. They [DOT]simply sent out their cards, got some of *them back, talked one way in one end of the country and another way in the other end; but they did nothing.
The climax of it all was the proposal to enlist 50,000 men for home defence. Fifty

thousand men to be taken out of productive industry at a time when it was believed that productive industry required all the . help that it could get; taken out of productive industry, but not sent to the firing line. How many (months did the Government spend on that project, and what was its result? Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce think that the Government is justified before this country in spending the time between June of last year and June of this year in talking one thing and doing a different thing; in talking action, but pursuing inaction? Is that his way of winning the war? And to-day, when there is placed before this House a suggestion that the power of Parliament is exhausted, that we hold no authority from the people of Canada, and that when we are imposing upon the people of Canada a measure, which, however necessary, however patriotic it may be, is still a most burdensome measure, we should ask the authority of the people to impose that measure; we are told that this suggestion is most unpatriotic because it would mean delay. It is right for the Government to delay, to walk up and down, to go round and round, for twelve long months; but it is absolutely unpatriotic for the leader of an Opposition to suggest that the people of Canada shall rule-because it might mean a delay of three months.
Now let me touch on the references made by the hon. gentleman to the province of Quebec. The province of Quebec has not sent as many men to the front, in proportion to population, as other provinces have. That is to be regretted. My right hon. friend thinks that the blame for the inaction of the province of Quebec-assuming that there has been inaction-rests upon whom? Upon the Government of the country? Oh, no; the blame rests upon the leader of the Opposition, the man from whom the majority of the people of Canada took the responsibility of office in 1911, the man who has held no responsibility of office since that time. He, we are told, is the man to blame, if blame there is, for the state of affairs in the province of Quebec, while the Government has no responsibility in the matter. In my humble judgment, a government constituted as this Government is, whose members from the province of Quebec were elected as being opposed, not to conscription fherely, but to military or naval service on behalf of the Empire-a Government with these men in its councils, supported by their colleagues from Quebec, who represent within a fraction of half the people of that province and number within ten of half its representation in

this House, must carry the responsibility for failure to recruit in the province of Quebec, and any lack of military enthusiasm in that province must fairly rest upon the shoulders of this Government, whose members are opposed, not only to conscription, but absolutely to military service.
The question before the House is serious; it is serious beyond measure. Surely, if there is danger of division, in this country, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said there was; although he brushed it aside lightly, it was a small thing-if there is a possibility that one of the provinces of this Dominion is likely to be opposed to the policy which is about to be undertaken; and if it is the fact-and the right hon. gentleman said it was the fact-that the leader of the Opposition is responsible for public opinion in the province of Quebec, would it not be reasonable, would it not be common sense for the Prime Minister and his colleagues to take the recommendation of the leader of the Opposition?

If the facts are as the
Minister of Trade and Commerce says they are-I do not say these are the facts; he says it-that is a reason why the proposal of the leader of the Opposition should be accepted by this Government in the interest of the wellbeing of the country, in the interest of its unity and therefore of its strength.
In speaking on this question I have dealt with it from the standpoint of voluntary enlistment and of the failure of voluntary enlistment in this country, and of the necessity, if necessity there is, for the introduction of this conscription measure. I think it only right to place before the House certain facts in regard to the measure of voluntary enlistment that is going on in Canada to-day, voluntary enlistment that is going on not because of the efforts of our Government but in spite of the efforts of our Government. I have here the latest issue of of the sheet called The Canadian Patriotic Fund, and I find a statement showing that the total enlistments in Canada for the Canadian Expeditionary Force for the month of January, 1917, were 7,721; for February, 7,644; for March, 6,648; for April, 5,420, a total of 27,433; or for one year, if continued at the same rate, 72,299. I note that a despatch from Kingston says that "456 recruits signed up in the Third Military District during the last two weeks." I say, in spite of this Government, and not because of it.
I desire to draw the attention of the House to an item which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of a day or two ago to the [DOT]effect that the enlistments in the city of Ottawa had fallen to a certain figure and the reason was because the enlistment office for the artillery service had been closed up. They had refused, during two weeks of the period to accept any recruits for the artillery service. It appears to me that when we have the evidence of the number of Tecruits during the preceding period, and when we have the evidence that this Government refused to accept recruits for any branch of the service here in this capital city of Ottawa, the Government has no right to say that voluntary enlistment is a failure in Canada or that people of Canada are lacking in their enthusiasm in support of this war.

speechtext:
I notice that the British Government comes in conveniently when my hon. friends desire to escape from a difficult situation, but it appears to me that if the casualties at the front are as they are reported to be, and there is no doubt they are, this Government would not be placing the British Government at any disadvantage if they accepted all the artillery recruits that offered and gave them the training that is necessary for efficiency in the artillery service. I am still compelled to believe that the closing up of the recruiting office in Ottawa, and the refusal of artillery recruits, was rather in the line of emphasizing the necessity of this Military Service Bill than of satisfying the demands of the British Government.
No one is more disappointed than I am that the Government should have felt it necessary at this stage of the proceedings to say to the country that their policy of voluntary enlistment had" broken down. There is, after all, something of inspiration in the idea of a man who volunteers, of men who, of their own good-will have left house and home, farm and land, wife, children and friends and have taken upon themselves, for their own credit and for the-honour of their country, the responsibility and sacrifice of the war. There is some-

thing insipiring in that, something to be proud of and Canada has reason to be proud that so many of her citizens have taken that position and have done her that measure of honour. It is a matter of the deepest regret to me as one citizen of this country, and as a member of this Parliament, that we are not going forward in the same line and to the same result.
While I say that, I also take the position, which I have taken in this House in times past-and I think I was the only member in the House to take it-that universal compulsory service was the only logical service under such conditions as prevail in the world at the present time. I believe that universal military service is the logical and efficient method of bringing to beaT the full strength of our country under present circumstances and conditions. Given a proper measure of universal military service, and there is equality in the distribution of the burden, an equality that does not exist in the case of voluntary service. While voluntary service has tremendous advantages in many ways, it has the disadvantage that the, willing horse carries the whole load. It is only fair that every horse should carry his share of the load. It is only on the principle of equality of service-of absolute equality of service-that the compulsory principle will be recognized or accepted. It is the only principle that is fair. If there is not equality of service under the compulsory principle, then, instead of i't (being a, democratic method of meeting a great emergency, it becomes an instrumeent of tyranny and unfairness in every particular.
The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) used the words " selective conscription ", and the Prime Minister explained that he was not able to adopt the Militia Act now on the statute-book because it did not contain the selective principle, and the selective principle must be provided for by special legislation. In the adoption of this selective principle there is vast room for anything but fairness in the administration of the Compulsory Service Bill. In that provision for selective conscription, it appears to me, there rests the greatest reason for objecting to the measure as it appears before the Hpuse. I have said in this House before, and I say again, that the great necessity to win this war is able-bodied men on the firing line, and any provision or measure before the House that takes the view that equal service can be rendered by an able-bodied

man in any other capacity, takes a view that I for one cannot agree with. And when I see a measure brought before the House as this measure is and advocated as this is, I am compelled to say that I do not look upon it as such a conscription measure as I would be willing to support.
To deal with a certain provision pf the Bill; It is provided, as the Prime Minister has told us, that there shall be a Board of selection, a Board of appeal, which amounts to a Board of selection, and this Board of appeal shall be absolutely independent- that is to say it will be absolutely irresponsible, absolutely irresponsible. In other words, that Board will express the sentiment of the men who compose it, who again will express the sentiment of the people amongst whom they live, And it is provided that this Board shall grant a certificate of exemption on the ground:
That It is expedient in the national interest that the man should, instead of being employed in military service, be engaged in other work in which he is habitually engaged.
That is to say, this irresponsible Board has all the authority of this Parliament to say: this man shall go and this man shall stay. There is neither let nor hindrance, there is neither direction nor suggestion, and this Parliament is asked to support that measure and call it a measure of conscription. It is a measure of conscription, but not a measure of conscription as I would feel able to support.

It is the business of the Prime Minister to bring in a measure that will be fair, and let me suggest to the Prime Minister and his friends that this is a responsibility resting upon their shoulders just as the administration of Canada's affairs in this war have rested on their shoulders, and I think they are
under a great mistake if they think that that responsibility is one thaf can be treated with levity.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman does not feel that he owes any duty to this Government, does he not owe a duty to the country to make suggestions?

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: I aim discharging my duty to the country according to my best judgment. Let me show how this provision will work out. In the part of the country where I live, where we have sent more men to the war in proportion to population than have been sent from any other part of the Dominion of Canada, where the men on homesteads, on the side lines, on the back streets, have gone in their thousands, and every day brings out its toll of casualties, carrying death and wounds into every side line and into, almost every house and cottage-we knew something of war in that part of the country, anid when you talk of conscription we want to know what it means. We have been led- to believe that a conscription measure would be fair to the country, and as we have done our duty, in a measure, so it would compel the people in other parts of the country to do their duty.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
Now, that is the kind of conscription measure I want to see, but that is not the kind of conscription measure my hon. friend has brought down, because when a board is appointed in the city of Edmonton, where the people have gone to the war and where the sentiment is in favour of maintaining our position in the firing line, and a man is called up and he appeals, the board will naturally say: Well, your neighbours have gone and you must go. That is what we would expect of a conscription measure in that part of. the country. That is to say, in our part of the country those who have not gone would be compelled to go. But shift that position down into the good province of Ontario, in some of its localities, or into the neighbouring province of Quebec, or possibly into the Maritime Provinces; you will find localities in all of those provinces where the people have not very enthusiastically volunteered for active service overseas, where the sentiment of the people is not favourable to such military service, and you have your tribunal there, just as you

have it in Alberta, and a young man appeals from the call and goes before this its authority under this provision to permit the man to remain they would he chased out of the country. The result would be that, we at Edmonton, who have sent of our best, and who have sent so many of them, will have to send still more, and those who have sent none will still send none, under this provision as it stands. This provision bears the closest possible relationship, in sentiment and idea, to those National Service cards, which were drawn up for an express purpose, and worded so that the man who believed in conscription was told " This is the beginning of conscription " and the man who did not believe in conscription was told that it certainly did not mean conscription, and we have the evidence of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny) on that point. We have a Bill that, to the people of Alberta, means conscription, but to the people of other parts of the country means just as much conscription as they want, and just the way they want it. That is not the kind of measure I would call a conscription Bill, and is not the kind of provision that I think is required to meet the Hun at the gate. It is not the way to do honour to this country and credit to the Government which brought it forward. I do not know, but it may be that this Bill has some resemblance to some Bill in England, or some measure passed in the United States. I can only say that we are legislating for Canada according to the conditions of Canada, and legislation that may be absolutely adapted to the conditions in England is not necessarily adapted to the conditions in Canada. Legislation which is adapted to the United States may not be adapted to our country. In case this legislation should be modelled on the English Bill, let me give the House some information as to how the English Bill is administered, and ask their opinions as to how they would be pleased to have similar -administration in Canada. I read in the Toronto Saturday Night of June 16th, an article from England written by an English correspondent, Lacey Amy: He speaks of the conditions in England, and- particularly of the conditions surrounding the enforcement of the conscription measure there. He says:
Tribunals all through the country continue to hanil out exemptions to huntsmen, variety artists, store managers, clerks, luxury manufacturers, frankly declaring that their mission is "to protect local industry". One district alone fMr. Oliver.]
granted 30,000 exemptions during the past fourteen weeks.
Even the Government joined the Freedom League. Only a few departments are not still to a large extent manned by eligibles with influence. In this 34th month of the war it is still the custom to hand a list of names to a branch of a department with orders to And places for them. A regiment is permitted to retain at home its football players and runners and boxers. The great markets of London

Smithfleld, Covent Garden, Billingsgate and the rest:-phave scarcely been touched, because their combing out was left to committees of themselves and they have been unable to agree.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, if that is the way they like to have it in England, it is not the way we like to have it here, and if this measure is modelled on the terms of the British measure, and if thesd are the results of the British measure, I say this is not a conscription Bill, according to my judgment, and is not entitled to my support.
There is this further feature of the volunteer system: that if a man volunteers, he does so for reasons of his own. He takes his chance. He accepts what he gets in the way of treatment, or casualties, or whatever it may be, and we who stand here, legislating for Canada in some measure, can carry the responsability lightly. But if we, by legislation, reach out our hand, take that man forcibly from his business and his family, bring him under military control, and send him into the firing line, it is for us to see in every step taken that every safeguard is afforded, and every justice meted out to him. In looking back over the part taken by Canada in this war since August, 1914, I regret to say that I cannot sec in the administration of our affairs, that spirit of fair play and of consideration for what is right and just that I would require to see in a government in whose hands I would entrust a measure of conscription of men.
I will not delay the House on the point, but I have here a clipping from the Montreal Star, a special cable from London, England, May 29th, by their correspondent, F. A. Mackenzie. Mr. Mackenzie has been at the front, and he states as follows:-
My visit to the base more than ever convinced me that we are suffering both at the London and French bases from over-systematization, which maintains thousands of unnecessary clerks, docking, indexing, the precise writing systems. The fault is not with the officers who are administering. I strongly urge the Dominion Government to have the system rigorously simplified in order to prevent the present staffs being overwhelmed by red tape and routine.
The dissolution of certain old battalions doing excellent service has been necessary.
The divisional staffs asked me to try and remove the impression prevailing in some parts

of Canada that the battalions were broken up because inefficient and unsatisfactory. Among them are several considered among the pick of the army. The necessity which compels the disintegrating of the veteran battalions with brilliant records and splendid esprit is considered deplorable. One dissolved battalion held a funeral service and the men erected a tombstone "To commemorate the last resting place of the 48th Battalion, raised by patriotism February, 1915, destroyed by politics May, 1917."	'
Further on he concludes:
The armies are heartily sick of politics, believing the politicians a curse to the service in their intrigues, forcing a number of unsuitable men into posts.
Such a record does not seem to me to warrant us in placing in the hands of this Government the power of life and death, of honour or dishonour, over our people by the tens of thousands.
This Government that comes to us with this conscription measure, and assumes to itself that, because it proposes conscription, therefore ^ it wants to win the war, when because of its course, of its action and of its inaction in carrying forward Canada'.- effort to win the war, conscription has to be resorted to. In, this as in every other case I am in favour of prompt and effective action. If a Government holding a mandate from the people believed in its wisdom that it was necessary to introduce a measure of conscription, it would be its duty to introduce such a measure, and to enforce it, if it could enforce it. But that is not the position; this Parliament holds no authority from the people. It was elected in September, 1911, for a period of five years; to-day it sits here, self-elected, but confirmed in ' position by the authority of the Imperial Parliament. It is competent for the Government to dissolve Parliament and appeal to the country, but in the Governor General s address at the opening of the House it was announced that such "was not the intention of the Government; that a further extension of the life of Parliament was to be arranged. On the Order Paper to-day is a notice that the Government purposes introducing a resolution for-the extension of the life of Parliament. We of the Opposition cannot command the Government. We know that we hold no mandate from the people; that our authority, so far as the people are concerned, was exhausted in October last. We see that the Government proposes still further to extend the life of Parliament; that it does not intend to go to the people for authority. Under those circumstances, the only way in which the authority of the
people can be secured is by the adoption of the amendment offered by the leader of the Opposition.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that he is is favour of conscription, but that fee would not entrust it to this Government. Will he say whether he would entrust conscription to the leader of the Opposition?

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: If the leader of the Opposition became leader of the Government, I certainly would.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman would entrust the enforcement of conscription to one who is altogether opposed to conscription.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: I do not know that he is altogether opposed to conscription.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: I heard him say here to-day that if his amendment is adopted and it is agreed to by the country, he would be a party to assisting the enforcing of conscription.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: But he is opposed to conscription. Would the hon. gentleman, then, entrust such a measure to him?

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
I certainly would entrust to the leader of the Opposition, if he were leader of the Government, the authority to enforce conscription, believing that he would enforce it if it were the law of the country and if the people had declared for it. But the leader of the Opposition and others on this side of the House are not prepared to take the responsibility of supporting a conscription measure when, having usurped the authority of the people, we sit here by our own authority, not by the authority of the people. 'That is the position that we want thoroughly defined. If the Liberal party stands for anything it stands for the rule of the majority of the people. We believe in responsible government, but when a Government that is absolutely not responsible to the people, and which holds office without regard to the people, brings forward a measure which lays a burden upon all the people, then all the people have a right to be heard with regard to that measure before it is put in force. That is what we-say, and that is all we say.
The leader of the Opposition has said that if a majority of the people are for conscription he will do his part in seeing that the law is carried out. I noticed how lightly the Minister of Trade and Commerce considered the authority of the people; it struck me that that certainly was good Tory doc-

trine. The fact that this Parliament did not hold authority from the people was a matter of the smallest possible consideration. We were Parliament, and because we were Parliament we should exercise our authority according to our judgment. If the military enthusiasm of our people declined, and if, because of the mismanagement of the Prime Minister in his leadership, our men at the front were not being supported, then we must make the people go-because we were Parliament.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
My hon. friend said just now that this Parliament had usurped the authority of the people. Does my hon. friend not believe that when the members of Parliament unanimously extended the life of Parliament for one year in order to ' avoiil bitter contest during the war the people in vast majority cordially approved that action?
Mr. OLIVER,: I do not know whether they did or not. We were careful not to take any chances on their doing it; we simply elected ourselves. I am not arguing that there was not at that time good and sufficient reason for the action that we took.
I	am arguing that because we took that action at that time is not a reason why we should take_ the same action again. Having taken the law into our own hands; having set ourselves up in a position independent of the people, we should, before forcing this measure upon them, submit it to their judgment and obtain their opinion upon it.
The leader of the Opposition drew attention in some measure to the condition of the House itself, aside from the fact that its term had expired and that the authority of the people, so far as we were concerned, had been exhausted. Taking the House as of 221 members, 9 seats are vacant by death,
II	by resignation, and 5 by reason of the members being unavoidably absent. There are two double seats: that is, two members each sit for two seats.
There are under military orders and pay 26 members of this House. These men under the military law are subject to service and entitled to pay therefor. I maih-tain^ that that is in effect an infraction of the independence of Parliament, whether it 13 inside the law or not. I am not criticising either the man or the military service, but it goes without saying that no matter who he is or how great the service he may render, the member of Parliament who is under military orders and receiving military pay is not in the position an independent member of Parliament should be in. He is 
not, as a matter of fact, an independent member of this House.
There are in this House, if I am correct in my count, 20 seats which are represented by men who were elected absolutely on the principle of opposition to Imperial Military service. It is this House, with this composition, that is to enforce conscription. Is it any wonder that the Conscription Bill is of the character that it is? We have had an administration of our military affairs since the war began that has not been to the credit of Canada, and I am one of those who believe that the influence of those men in the Cabinet and outside who were absolutely opposed to Canada's participation in Great Britain's wars is one of the great reasons why we have not had a more effective administration of our affairs in this war.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister in his Speech a few days ago suggested what might happen to members of this House if the Conscription Bill were not passed. What does he think will happen to members of this House and of this Government who armed the men in the trenches at Ypres with rifles that would not shoot under stress of circumstances, and who kept them armed with those rifles and sent other men into the trenches armed with the same rifles for one long year after they had it on the authority of the British general that the rifle was inefficient? Perhaps it was not the influence of those who were opposed to Canada's participation in the wars of the Empire that was responsible for that condition, but undoubtedly that was the con-[DOT] dition that did exist, and for that condition this Government is responsible, and it will be well for other members of the Government and other members of Parliament if they can show that it was those who were opposed to Canada's participation in the war who were responsible for the blood of the men who died at Langemarck and Zille-beck because the Government armed them with a rifle that they knew to be inefficient.
In a House of 221 members we have 9 seats vacant by death, 11 by resignation, 2 double seats, 5 unavoidably absent, 26 under military orders and pay, 20 elected to oppose military service for the Empire, 2 are under-secretaries, and 2 occupy special positions without pay, but with allowances,
I suppose; I speak of the Director of National Service and the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Green), who is now acting for the Government in the coal strikes. There is a total of 19 seats which are either vacant or the representatives of

which are not in the position of an absolutely independent member of Parliament. In a House of Commons of 235 seats, as it would be after a general election, there would be 79 as above, 22 unrepresented, and 8 over represented, a total of 109 seats,or nearly one-half not represented as they ought to be. It is this Parliament, which has outlived the term for which it was elected, with nearly one-half of the seats unrepresented or represented by members who are not in the position they should be in, that proposes to put through a Conscription Bill compelling 100,000 of our men to give military service at the front, under the plea and pretense that the loyalty and military enthusiasm of our people have failed us in this time of stress. This conscription measure is brought forward as an excuse and apology for the Government's failure to discharge their duties and responsibilities for the honour of Canada and the safety of the Empire.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the House was very much .surprised this afternoon when the right hon. leader of the Opposition moved an amendment to the second reading of this Bill, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton. We have listened to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) for an hour and three quarters endeavouring to show in the first place that the Bill does not go far enough, and in his next breath telling the House and country that the Bill is an iniquitous measure because it will tear the son from his mother and the husband from his wife. He tried to show that the Bill was not a Compulsory Service Bill, that in its working out it would practically defeat its own ends, and yet his chief condemnation of the Government tonight was that the Bill would have the dire effect upon the manhood of the country to which I have alluded. He says he is in favour of compulsory service, and always has been, and then deliberately seconds an amendment which amounts to a hoist for the Bill which would bring in compulsory service.
And he refuses, even though invited by the Prime Minister, to make a single suggestion to improve the Bill. He would send the Bill as it stands to the people to be ratified by the people, and would hand over the administration of it to the leader of the Opposition who is absolutely opposed to it; and yet he refuses to give any suggestion for the improvement of the Bill. To my mind, such a position is illogical and untenable.
Another point that my hon. friend makes is that this Bill is weak because, forsooth, Alberta and some other provinces, my own province for instance, have already contributed very liberally under the voluntary system, and it will take from these provinces certain individuals while allowing individuals in other provinces to escape. And why? Because he says the Bill provides for administration by an independent board which he chooses to call ' irresponsible." What would he have said had the Government brought down a Bill to be administered, for instance, by the Minister of Militia or by some special committee of this House? He would at once have declared that it was a Bill for a political end, that it should have been entrusted to the courts. But because the Government bring down a Bill to be administered by the courts of the land, he says, forsooth, that this is an "irresponsible" way to administer the Bill. He might as well say that the courts of the land, from the Supreme Court and the Exchequer Court down to the police court, are irresponsible and do not administer the ordinary laws properly day after day. The very same men, the judges of the county courts, the judges of the Supreme Court, are the men chosen by the Government to administer the exclusion clauses of the Bill; and I repeat, his reflection upon these men must carry with it the inference that they are incapable of administerihg the ordinary laws of the land. Otherwise, his criticism means absolutely nothing; it is merely a captious criticism.
Referring to the munitions work, he took the Government to task because, he alleges, early in the year 1916, the Government and the Minister of Militia of that time had prevented the men, skilled workers, engaged in the manufacture of munitions, from enlisting. I have not heard of a single case of a man who insisted upon enlisting being denied that privilege.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: I was not here when the hon. member for Edmonton spoke. Did he say that there was interference with the men employed in munitions enlisting?

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
Yes.
Sir SAM 'HUGHES:	It is an absolute
falsehood.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: I only read from Hansard what the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) said.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) said something to the effect that there was a conspiracy 'between the Prime Minister and the Minister of

Militia of that time to prevent individuals from enlisting and to keep them in the munition factories. That is a most unfair criticism of the Government; for the hon. gentleman himself, from his place in the House in 1915, and also I think in this very session of 1916, attacked, condemned, and maligned the Government because it was not assisting the Mother country in getting out munitions and was not giving sufficient support to the men at the front who at that time were suffering because munitions were not supplied in sufficient quantities. He knows that the one thing needed in 1915, when our boys went in at the front, was munitions; the thing that caused the slaughter at various points in Flanders was that they had not heavy artillery and munitions. And what gives the British at the front the advantage to-day? The tremendous quantity of munitions. And how have they been brought up to that point? By Canada, the United States, and the Motherland bending their skill and energy to their manufacture. The hon. member knew very well, when he made his unfair criticism, that the British Government brought men back from the front-thousands of them-to * put them at work on munitions rather than allow them to remain in the front line. He seeks-and I consider it a most unfair and unkind criticism-and makes it an object of petty, picayune political attack, to compare the heroism of the men in the factory with that of the men on the firing line. We know that the men at the front, willing' to lay down their lives, and hundreds of them making that last great sacrifice, are rendering to the country a service that can never be too highly appreciated. At the same time, it must be admitted that the men in certain walks of life can do their country a great service for the time being by sending to the men at the front the support of munitions. Let me give an instance. A young McGill student from my own city, skilled in analysing steel, enlisted as a private and was on his way to the front. But the former Minister of Militia got hold of him, and that young man is now in the Ordnance Department filling a position as a skilled engineer testing steel in the manufacture of ordnance, a thing that very few men in Canada understand. Would the hon. member for Edmonton take that young man out of the Ordnance Department and send him to the front? We on this side who differ with the hon. gentleman in political matters have always regarded him as an honest, rugged fighter, whatever we may 
have thought of his opinions. But his criticism to-night did not do him credit, nor do I think his constituents will approve the stand he has taken.
The hon. gentleman also referred to the failure of the voluntary system, and he very glibly tells us that the responsibility lies at the door of the Government. If this Government is entirely responsible for the failure of the voluntary system, then it follows absolutely that this Government and its supporters alone Were engaged in the promotion of volunteering. But that is not true; the hon.- gentleman and I know that it is not true. We can speak with assurance when we say that throughout Ontario and the West, and 'throughout Eastern Canada we know, but not with the same personal knowledge, both Liberals and Conservatives in every walk of life have joined hands in the work of making the voluntary system a success. We on this side have never hesitated to give credit to our Liberal friends in the West, and I could name them by the score, who have done great service in that line. But when the hon. gentleman stands in his place and seriously, on this solemn occasion, tries to make the House and the country believe that this Government alone is responsible for the voluntary system, he acknowledges that he and his friends have failed to do anything for that system.
He complains that this Government took no action between last June and this June, and this, he said repeatedly, is the time when the volunteer system failed. He says the Government should have taken action last June, and yet says that the Government having delayed for twelve months, it should delay for three months more, and perhaps not pass the measure at all. In one breath he charges the Government with not proposing conscription a year ago and in the next, with all his power, eloquence and influence, he seeks to delay the matter for another three or four months.
If the Government was at fault, as he says it was, it is his duty, and the duty of every citizen of the country, to see that the thing is done now. Delay is not going to improve it. As a matter of fact, he knows, and I think the country at large knows, that there was an earnest effort on the part of the Government to avoid conscription. Why? In the first place, I think we had a decided pride in the fact that Canada had done so well under the voluntary system. I want to pause a moment to pay a tribute to Canada, to my country, for the splendid manner in which it has responded to the

call in this great war under the voluntary system. I was hoping, as I am sure many others have 'been, that we would have been able to get the 500,000 men and stand out as the one country in the world that did not require compulsory service. But, unfortunately, for various reasons that has not been possible, and so the Government come down now, after exhausting every other effort to secure the men, with a compulsory measure. My hon. friend refuses to make any suggestions to improve this Bill. He chooses at this most critical time in the country's and the Empire's history, at this most critical time in the history of modern civilization, to enter on a course of destructive criticism and refuses to make a single constructive suggestion to help the Government, notwithstanding the fact that the sincerity of the Government in inviting such suggestions was conclusively shown by the fact that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister allowed this Bill to stand for several weeks after it was introduced in order to give the leader of the Opposition an opportunity of joining with him in a national, coalition Government. When my hon. friend seeks to cast a reflection upon the Prime Minister and his Government, he * has to reckon with that fact, and I believe that the country will properly weigh criticisms of that kind.
We are faced with a single condition. This war is either justifiable or it is not, it is either right or wrong, it should be sustained or it should be abandoned. That is the situation with which we are faced to-day. We have no choice except between these two courses. There is no middle course. Either we must sustain the men at the front by sending reinforcements or we must abandon them. There is, I repeat, absolutely no middle course. It ill behooves us as members of this Parliament to stand in our places here, as the leader of the Opposition did this afternoon, go back to the Boer War,, or to the Drummond and Athabasca election and rake up all the political squabbles that have arisen in this country during the last twenty years. Such a proceeding is unnecessary and ill-timed. The thing for us to do is to face the conditions now. The conditions are clear, and again I say there is no middle course. If we admit, as I think we must admit, that our cause is a just one, and that we are battling for right against despotism, tyranny and brutal might, we dare not abandon the fight, we must not fail at this time, and we must concentrate our efforts upon bringing into play to the
utmost our national strength. This Bill presented by the Prime Minister is calculated to do that very thing, to bring into play the full strength of the manhood of the country.
My hon. friend from Edmonton, as did his leader this afternoon, raises the constitutional quibble-I have no other word to characterize it-that as a moribund Parliament we have no power, no mandate, and no right to go on with this measure until we have consulted the people. Let us look at the logic of that for one moment. Year after year the Finance Minister has been bringing before Parliament methods of financing which were equally as revolutionary as compulsory military service. Last year he brought in a new method of financing; this year he extends it. Certain hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House condemn these measures as too drastic and far reaching. Why did not the hon. member for Edmonton and his leader on those occasions demand that the Finance Minister submit these measures to the people; they were more revolutionary than this measure, because there is no question but what this Bill simply contains what has been on the statute book for the last fifty years. The hon. member for Edmonton smiles, but I will reach the clause again, although it has been read two or three times. Clause 61 of the Militia Act of 1868 is as follows:	,
Her Majesty may call out the militia, or any part thereof, for actual service-
Mark the words.
-either within or without the Dominion, at any time whenever it appears advisable so to do by reason of war, invasion, or insurrection, or danger of any of them.
My hon. friend from Edmonton and the leader of the opposition will no doubt say that it is perfectly true, but that there is no danger of invasion. I do not think that the member for Edmonton would urge that, because I frankly believe that he realizes the seriousness of this war, and that it really means invasion if it means anything at all. But if that argument is raised, I quote what the leader of the opposition said in this House on August 19, 1914. Here are his words;
Our territory is liable 'to attack and to invasion. Our shipping to Great Britain has been interrupted. England to-day is not engaged in an ordinary contest.
Could anything be clearer? The right hon. gentleman this afternoon urged seriously, and emphasized from his place in

the House, that he never believed we were in danger of invasion. He said in 1914, in the first war session:
Our territory is liable to attack and invasion, our commerce has been interrupted.
Again I call attention to the Act, in order that I may put this question for ever at rest:
Her Majesty may call out the militia, or any part thereof, for actual service, either within or without the Dominion at any time, whenever it appears advisable so to do by reason of war, invasion, or insurrection, or danger of any of them.
Surely that is clear enough. But there is another phase of the question that I would call the attention of the House to. Supposing it is admitted for the sake of argument that there was no danger of direct invasion, but supposing we found that our commerce was interrupted. What would be the result? The property of Canada is not all contained within Canada. Wherever there are ships carrying cargo from Canada, there lies the property of Canada, and wherever lies the property of Canada, in a ship or otherwise, there lies the duty of Canada to defend that property. If the Canadian Government and the Canadian people say: We will send our cargoes out in our ships, and the minute they pass the three-mile limit we will have no further interest in them, their sense of national responsibility is about as low as that of any nation that we call civilized. It is not the ease. The case is this, that wherever there is Canadian property, wherever there are Canadian lives or citizens, there lies Canadian duty and the duty of the Canadian Government to protect and defend them.
I wish to ask now this question:	Who
are particularly opposing this Bill? And I find, after careful thought, that there are two, or perhaps three elements. First, there is a section of organized labour, and I use the word "section" advisedly, a section of organized labour, because the sentiment is not by any means unanimous among the organized labour of Canada, who oppose the Bill, I shall refer to that later. Then there is almost a unanimous Quebec. I say almost because there are quite a large number of citizens of Quebec who are certainly in favour of this Bill and of prosecuting this war to a successful issue, and to these we give all honour and credit. But there is unquestionably a strong . sentiment in that province opposing it, which I shall review in a moment. Third, there is a miscellaneous group, the slacker, the individual who has a mis-

guided opinion that it is a sin to defend one's own family and hearth and rights, that in some way or other we should lie down and allow ourselves to be abused to any extent without offering any violence in return. There is that element, but I do not think they amount to much or have much influence in the upbuilding of the country.
Let me refer briefly to the situation in Quebec, and I hope to deal with it in all moderation and in a spirit of sincerity and kindness. I must Tefer, in connection with this subject, to an epoch-making event when Edward the Peacemaker consummated the entente cordiale_ between the two gteat-est democracies in the world, when they joined hands in the inspiring duty of preserving to the world those noble principles for which both had separately contended for many centuries. Sir, that was, I say, an epoch-making event which was welcomed by the democracies of the world as an evidence of the triumph of democracy over autocracy in the future history of events, and I think we can say this, that genuine and mutual were the efforts of the statesmen of both countries to bring that great event to a practical issue. But, sir, it rested with this great war to bring it to its ultimate result and effect, and this war has sealed that agreement, has sealed that Treaty, has sealed that understanding, with 10 p.m. the 'blood of the noblest sons of . the two nations, on the common field of battle. So in Canada, when war broke out, while we realized that there would undoubtedly be serious results, that there would be suffering, we welcomed to a certain degree this war, because we hoped it would for ever strike out of the national life of Canada the differences between the two great races in this country. I remember perfectly well how it was welcomed as an evidence of the good will of the two races in Canada, and we had hoped that now we could have a common ground upon which we could travel along side by side, in pursuance of our country's welfare. But, unfortunately, things- have occurred that have dissipated that hope. I wish to read to the House some words that fell from the lips of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) _at that time, inspiring .and graceful, so far as language is concerned. I suggest that the House .should listen to these words, because they have unquestionably the right ring to them, and while we are sometimes .mystified to harmonize the actions of the right hon. gentleman with his words, we at least must admire the sentiment expressed in them:-
