It is our duty, more pressing upon us than all other 'duties, at once, on this first day of this extraordinary session of the Canadian Parliament, to let Great Britain know, that there is in Canada but one mind and one heart and that all Canadians stand behind the Mother Country, conscious and proud that she has engaged in this war, not from any selfish motive, not for any purpose of aggrandizement, but to maintain untarnished the honour of her name, to fulfil her obligations to her Allies, to maintain her Treaty obligations, and to save civilization from the unbridled lust of conquest and domination.
I submit that these are noble words and noble sentiments that fell from the lips of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. But, I ask, what has happened in the last three years to change all this? What is there that makes the situation any different to-day? Has anything occurred in the past two or three years to make it less necessary that we should give our whole service to the Empire? Is there any reason why we should delay now,, whereas the right hon. gentleman then said " at once " we should do this or that in support of the Motherland? He went on to say:
Long have we enjoyed the benefits of British citizenship; to-day it is our duty to accept its responsibilities and its sacrifices.
In my estimation, in these words we have a complete answer to the right hon gentleman's opposition to this Bill. There are responsibilities that he must take, that every member of this House and every citizen of Canada must take. We have heard from his lips and also from those of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) the constitutional question of whether this Parliament has the power or right to proceed with the Bill. This country is ruled or governed by a responsible Parliament elected by the people. It is true that our term expired last October, but it was, by a unanimous vote of this House, in which both of these hon. gentlemen concurred, extended, and what for? Not to carry on the ordinary business of the country, but to carry on the business of this war. That was the underlying principle of the extension of Parliament, that the business of the war might be carried on. Will the right hon gentleman or my hon. friend from Edmonton say that this Bill is not calculated to advance the cause of the war? Will they say that it is not necessary? Will they say that we can delay for two or three months in securing reinforcements for the front? It is perfectly useless for them to say that we did not do our best in the past. The past is gone, we are dealing with the present and with the immediate future, our duty rests there and does not rest in the past, and no amount of criticism of the past will bring about the needed assistance at this time. There are certain arguments which have been advanced by those who are opposed to this measure, and I think they are pretty well summed up in a resolution passed in Montreal the other day. I will deal very briefly with a few of these utterances. In this resolution they say:
Prepared as we are to defend the territory of Canada against all foreign attacks, we are equally determined to defend the autonomy of Canada and the liberties of its citizens against every agression from within.
In other words, this is what is said: We are quite prepared to defend Canada from attack, but we are not prepared to do anything in the defending. In other words, supposing there was a band of outlaws loose in a neighbourhood, some of the people might congregate together for the common defence of the community; others would say: We will not take any part in the defence against these, outlaws until they attack our premises, nor until they come to our farms, our stores or our houses, then we may take measure of defence, but so long as they do not attack us on our own soil we will make no defence.
It seems to me that is a parallel ease. Here we are a nation among nations, a people among peoples, a democracy among democracies, and when the soul of democracy is attacked by the most villainous and brutal power the world ever developed, one of the greatest portions of that democracy, or nation among nations of democracies stands back and says, "No, we will go no further" until when, forsooth? "Until our own shores are attacked." That was the argument of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, and it is the argument set forth in this resolution from Montreal, in the province of Quebec. I contend that such an argument is absolutely untenable.
It is claimed by those same people that conscription violates the constitution. 1 have already set that at rest. Conscription does not violate the constitution, because one of the first Acts passed by this Confederated Dominion contains a clause for compulsory service within or without Canada, and I think that argument should be abandoned by those who are opposing this Bill, because it absolutely fails from end to end. They say it violates the constitution, and what do they suggest? The hon. gentleman from Edmonton suggests a refer-

endum. Where will he find, in. the whole constitution, authority for a referendum on a question of this kind? It is not there. Of course, we can create a system of referendum, and I have no particular objection to it, but we are living under a system of responsible Government by a representative Parliament, elected by the people. That responsibility is resting on us now, and this is not the time to discuss whether we are going to change our system, introduce re-ferendums, and amend our constitution. This is not the time to squabble about new policies. It is the time to take advantage, as I have already suggested, of the powers we have and to put them into execution. This resolution goes on:
We believe that all new efforts on the part of the nation should be directed to the sole object of re-organizing the economic forces of the country, and of supplying the allied nations, whose cause Canada has joined, England especially, with the foodstuffs which they so insistently ask for.
That is their idea of their full duty. In other words, it is suggested that Canada should devote all her attention to selling foodstuffs to the allied nations, to take the homely illustration I cited a moment ago, " We will not go out with the posse, but we will feed the posse at reasonable terms, we will not proceed to fight the Huns or stand in the way of their invasion and aggression, but we will gladly feed those who do the fighting - at profitable rates That is the argument, without any question. Another objection or suggestion was made by Edouard Monpetit, a professor in Laval University, who said that " Canada had done more than her share in the war, and that her moral obligation had been fulfilled." Reference is also made to the question of devoting our attention to supplying foodstuffs. There is no question that it is important, but if Canada emerges from this war with her honour intact and unsullied, but bankrupt, I contend she will be infinitely better off and richer in her national life than if she came out with hundreds of millions of dollars, reaped from the war, but failed, at this time, to do her part in sustaining the Empire.
I will refer, briefly, to another, phase of the argument advanced by labour advocates and draw attention to a few of their statements. I shall quote the official organ of the labour party in my own city. I have no objection to any responsible citizen advancing views adverse to my own, or to those which are held by the party to which I belong. 'It is perfectly right that they should do so, but I reserve the right to defMr. Stevens]
bate those views, and, if possible, to answer them. I wish to show that those among the trades unions of Canada who are opposing conscription are really not consistent in the action they are taking. At the outbreak of the war, the Dominion Trades and Labour Council inserted a clause in their report stating that organized labour was behind the Allies until they had gained a final and decisive victory. They admit the war is in the interests of democracy, and that the principles at stake are democratic. I will read an editorial in the British Columbia Federation, the. official organ of the Labour Party of Canada, written June 1, 1917, and, while in this article is an argument against conscription, nevertheless I want to quote it,. to show that they realize that this is a democratic war, in the interests of the best principles of democracy. The writer of the article says:
The old idea that the war was a natural consequence of trade, and that the present one had its origin solely in conflicting trade rivalries, has long since become so thoroughly shot to pieces, that it is no longer entertained except by the most- shallow and superficial thinkers. It is now very widely acknowledged that the terrible spectacle now being staged by a veritable world at war, is but the inevitable and deadly struggle between the despotism and autocracy of the older slavery (chattel and feudal) and the democratic tendency and spirit of the latter (the capitalist form). It is a struggle to the death between the political concept of the former, which was of necessity despotic and stationary, and the political concept of the latter, which is democratic and progressive.
In other words, this editorial writer properly contends that this war is one between autocracy represented by the German States, and democracy, represented by the Allies. Admitting that, they argue that conscription is an attempt to resurrect despotism. The whole case of labour organizations against conscription rests upon the one point, whether or not the measure of conscription before the country to-day is a despotic measure, reactionary and liable to introduce the old autocratic system. If that system can be proven, then it is wrong. If on the other hand, it can be demonstrated that it is rather a measure to support the- cause of democracy, then I say the last excuse of the labour representatives is removed. Democracy gives privileges to all classes pf the people. The democracy of France, of the United States, and of the British Empire, gives to the people of these countries the highest type of personal and national freedom that any country or any people ever enjoyed. b[one can gainsay that statement. If that be the

case, there goes with it the corresponding duty of defending those rights and privileges, and the democracy that gave them to us. The very basis of democracy is compulsory service.
If you accept the idealistic view of the socialist who is opposing conscription, you accept the view that every man should be placed by the State in the sphere in which he is to move from time to time. The extreme view of the democratic socialist is that the State must control the activities of every man in the State; that is the underlying and fundamental principle of their belief. Yet these very men deny that principle when it is applied to the defence of the democracy which they claim to uphold. The situation is clear and unanswerable:
If you accept the principles of democracy as advanced by the extreme democratic socialist, you accept the principle of compulsory service in various walks of life. To adopt compulsory military service, therefore, is actually to carry out the principle for which they so strongly stand.
It is argued that the people were not consulted. I ask the member for Edmonton and others who advance that argument: Was Belgium consulted when Germany invaded her territory? Was Serbia consulted? Were the people on the Lusitania consulted? Was Edith Cavell consulted? Was Captain Fryatt consulted? Were the members of families in Belgium consulted-not three years ago, but only last year-when they were separated and taken away to the worst kind of slavery in Germany? Were the common laws of humanity consulted on these occasions? It is contended that we should stand back and submit this proposal to an academic discussion throughout Canada, spend three or four months in deciding whether or not we should go ahead with it, while Germany with all her brutal force is-doing what? Consulting the con- . venience and comfort of the people with whom she is dealing? No; ruthlessly defying every law of humanity. The member for Edmonton and his leader suggest that these are times when we should engage in academic discussions; when we should quibble over principles; when we should debate whether such action is constitutional or unconstitutional; when we can afford to incur delay. The solemn duty rests upon those of us who are in Canada to do our part just as nobly, in our own limited way, as the boys at the front are, day after day and month after month, performing their duty. All this discussion, all this quibbling, all this political side-stepping, is wholly *out of place; I am tempted to characterize it as almost a disgrace to this Parliament.
We have heard a great deal about conscripting wealth. But those who advocate the conscription of wealth are unable to defipe what they mean by the conscripting of wealth. " The conscripting of wealth " is one of the most convenient political phrases that I have ever heard. It is almost a twin sister to the term " free food." It has no meaning; it has never been defined; no one seems to be willing to take responsibility for it. What has the Finance Minister been doing during the last two years but conscripting wealth? Hon. gentlemen who now say that we should conscript wealth, not more than three ot four weeks ago told the Finance Minister that he would ruin the industries of Canada, if he took too much of their profits. As a matter of fact, what is being done towards the conscripting of wealth? . Hon. gentlemen aTe familiar with what is being done; it is only necessary to reiterate what has already been said. Twenty-five per cent of excess profits of 7 to 15 per cent is taken by the Government. Of excess profits of 15 to 20 per cent, the Government takes 50 per cent, and of excess profits 20 to 100 per cent, the Government takes 75 per cent. Surely that is a fair step towards the conscription of wealth.
It may be said, with a certain degree of force, that we should have an income tax. The Minister of Finance told us that it would be necessary to bring down further taxation later, and that it was not wise to launch every type of taxation at once. The taxation which he has launched and which takes a portion of excess profits during war time is the fairest type of taxation ever brought down in this House-and it is sufficient for the time being. Next year- if necessary, perhaps this year- the Minister of Finance can bring forward further methods of taxation.
The argument of our friends in Quebec that Canada has done enough may be answered in this way. I wonder if those hon. gentlemen opposite who have declared very loudly that they are going to vote against this Bill-one or two of them have already stated on the floor of the House that we have done too much for the Motherland in this war-ever think of the gentleman who ought to be sitting alongside the member for Edmonton, our colleague, Dr. Beland? Do they remember that the doctor had been in France when war broke out, and that he cheerfully gave his services to the French and Belgian Governments



in order that he might aid the wounded and the dying? Do they remember that he and his wife were imprisoned, and that when his wife died the brutal Huns refused to give him an opportunity of seeing her on her death-bed? Not long ago a despatch stated that our colleague, after two or three years' imprisonment, lies at the point of death, and that he is not likely to survive much longer. ^If hon. gentlemen from Quebec who declare that they will oppose this Bill have forgotten the other atrocities and outrages that I have mentioned, have they forgotten their colleague, Dr. Beland? If they have, we have not.
Without any question, this is a war to defend the most cherished principles of democracy. If we fail in this struggle because of lack of attention to the duties that now present themselves, then, Sir, that democracy fails. To hear the arguments of some of the gentlemen who have spoken throughout the country-not on the floor of the House, I admit-one would almost think that it would be better to live under the Hun than to adopt compulsory service in Canada in defence of democracy. That was really the substance of his argument. It is inconceivable to me how anyone can consider such a thing for a moment. If we do not measure up at this time to the proper height, then democracy receives its death blow. There is only one course before us in my opinion, and that is to accept the Bill. If the Bill has weaknesses-, let us point them out, as the Prime Minister says. In Committee of the Whole-we are here discussing the principle-I shall cheerfully join with other members in a careful consideration of each clause. If we can strengthen the Bill let us do it; if we can make it more rigid, let us do so. If we can define any points more clearly, let us do that also. No one knows better than the hon. member for Edmonton that it is absolutely impossible to get what he calls an equitable Bill. He says if this Bill was equitable and fair he would accept it. He knows very wel-l that there is no law on the statute book that is absolutely impartial. We can only get as near to that ideal as the intelligence of this House will permit, and it behooves the hon. gentlemen and every other member of this House to make this Bill the best of its kind that can be produced.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a great deal this evening about the Hun at the gate. My hon. friend who has just preceded me (Mr. Stevens) represents Vancouver, ofie of

the gates of Canada. My constituency lies near the other gate, and the Eastern gate is nearer the Hun than the Western gate. Speaking on behalf of my people, I can assure you, Sir, that we near the Eastern gate of Canada do not fear the Hun.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
Because we can meet him as we have met him before. I come from a province where something was done for the British flag, before British Columbia and other provinces in the west were in existence. There might have been no British flag in America at the present time but for Quebec; that question was settled over a century ago and there is official evidence testifying to it. I represent a constituency which is largely French-speaking, although it has a large proportion of English-speaking . settlers too, descendants of the United Empire Loyalists, and I know, I am speaking for them in the remarks I shall make tonight. I am, according to Parliamentary doctrine, as much a representative of Vancouver as a representative of Bonaventure. Once a member is elected to this house he represents the whole of Canada, and it is as a member representing the whole of Canada that I intend to sneak this evening and not on behalf of one locality or one province.
I was born in the province of Quebec. My ancestors came here nearly three centuries ago, and I hope to die and be buried on Canadian soil. I belong to this country and am faithful and loyal to it, and since the outbreak of war I have done everything it was possible for me to do in company with ministers of the Crown and others to stimulate recruiting and bring about the effort which I think Canada should make in the great contest before us. A great deal of interest is being taken at the present time in the situation in the province of Quebec. The leader of the Opposition, in his magnificent speech this afternoon, pointed out some reasons why recruiting had not been very active in that province. Many other reasons could have been given, but the chief reason is that recruiting in the province of Quebec was badly handled from the .start. Even now it !is not too late to adopt proper methods. If this measure were withdrawn and recruiting was carried on in the province of Quebec ,as it should be, by General Lessard, Colonel Blondin and other compatriots of the people of the province, I am sure we should get satisfactory results. Suppose, for a moment, that French-Canadians had been sent into Alberta, or Ontario, or British Columbia, and had asked the English-speaking people

there to listep to French recruiting addresses, and to join French battalions, and practise French military manoeuvres, what results do you think, Sir, would have been obtained in those English-speaking provinces? Men are men, and blood is thicker than water. The recruiting has not been properly handled in the province of Quebec. When Colonel Blondin undertook to raise a battalion he adopted the proper method. He was accompanied by General Lessard, who is one of the best men we have in Canada and should have been employed from the very start, but why he was not, we do not know. They went into those parts of the province where they were likely to get recruits, and the results they obtained were very satisfactory. Col. Blondin declared that he stopped recruiting because of the introduction of conscription, not because recruiting was a failure in the province of Quebec.
I was sent to this House to help administer the affairs of this country as best I could. I have sat now for 18 years in Parliament; I have seen 179 members come and go, and a score of Cabinet ministers; I have seen a half dozen men occupy the Speaker's chair; I have voted for all kinds of measures, for the buildings of railways, and for the opening up of Canada in every part. I have taken as deep an interest in the province of New Brunswick as in the province of Quebec, as deep an interest in Ontario as in the Maritime and Western Provinces. After 18 years faithful service I claim to stand before you to-night, Sir, as a Canadian who has done his duty well not only by his own people but by the people at large. I consider it my duty now to say that I have no mandate, and have not been authorized to vote in favour of this Military Service Bill which has been introduced by the Government. I want the Allies to win this war. Everybody in the province of Quebec and everybody in Canada wants the Allies to win. There is not a man, woman, or child in this country that does not want us to win the war. Our Bed Cross associations, Patriotic, and Belgian Belief Funds are doing everything possible for the soldiers, and to all these our people are contributing with results that have done Canada so much honour. Canada has sent forward a volunteer army of nearly 400,000 men. In the early days of August, 1914, the Government began in fear and trembling by offering a division of 30,000. Was that the extent to which they wanted Canada to participate in this war? They were not pro-
155i
phets, but they felt that Canada could well send 30,000 men at that time. When Parliament met in the old building in August, 1914, members from the province of Quebec and every other province unanimously assented to all the measures brought down and cheerfully voted for every dollar that was asked for by the Government to win. the war. We went into it as a band of brothers because we wanted Canada to figure prominently in this war for the great, principles of humanity and -freedom which we all have at heart. Why was this done?' What did the leaders say? What did we all say in our recruiting speeches? What did the Minister of Finance say when he appeared with me in. the Bussell theatre in the city of Ottawa? lie said that Canada's participation in the war was entirely voluntary, and every man had to settle with his own conscience the question of enlistment. That was the appeal that was made throughout the country; we appealed to the hearts of the people, and that was why we met with such success. Now the Government brings down a measure of conscription in a moribund and defunct parliament, in which 20 or more seats are vacant and several members away. We have overrun our term by several months.
If this Government wish to serve the Allies, if they wish to make more effective the participation of Canada in the war, if they are sincere in favouring participation, there is only one course for them to take, and that is to appeal to the people, to trust the people.
This Bill was announced when recruiting was going on at the rate of about six or seven thousand a month, and this notwithstanding that the Minister of the Interior found so great scarcity of labour for our prairie farms that he felt it necessary to send to the United States to bring help. Surely, this rate of recruiting was satisfactory. But it will all be wiped off if you have this conscription measure.
We are told that there is opposition to this measure in the province of Quebec. So there is. But in many other provinces also there is opposition to it. That opposition exists chiefly because this measure is introduced as a change of the rules after the game has begun. We went into this war voluntarily. The Prime Minister has just returned from the Imperial War Conference, and he has told us that nothing new in respect of the autonomy of the Overseas Dominions was touched upon or decided, because it was understood that that autonomy was to be preserved. If

ever there was a question coming before the House on which the autonomy of the people must be preserved, it is a question in which the liberty of the subject is affected. If you want Canadians throughout Canada to participate actively in this war, do not attempt coercion, but appeal to the big heart of the nation, appeal to their patriotism and their better spirit; do not come down with the big stick and have half the population chasing the other half.
How is this measure going to be enforced? Are you going to jail two or three hundred thousand people? These people consent to the active participation of Canada in the war, tout they are not going to be drummed into it. Gladstone, when he had to deal with Ireland, always said that coercion was of no use. Why is Ireland being left aside in the conscription measure in Britain? Because Lloyd George declared that he would not lose time in trying to enforce conscription in Ireland until Ireland was free to accept it voluntarily. Let the Irish question be settled, and Ireland w'ill accept conscription and will do what she has always done, and Scotland too-and England as well, but never more than Ireland or Scotland- she will send forth to uphold the Empires cause the best soldiers that Britain has had to support that cause throughout the world.
We want this matter dealt with fairly. We want to take the people into our confidence. We want dissolution of this Parliament, that we may go hack to the men who sent us here, the men who. are to pay the money and who ultimately will have to shed their blood. We want England io be victorious in this war, and we want Canada to participate, but in order that Canada may participate most effectively, we must go back to the people and go hack immediately; we must appeal to their 'best feeling, hut not try coercion, because coercion will not bring results.
Those who favour this coercion measure say they do not want to go to the country. And why? Because, they say, if it were submitted to the people it would be rejected. If rejected, it would be because the people do not like to be tyrannized over, and tbis is nothing more or less than an act of tyranny. What the Prime Minister should have done-and he ought to know it better than I or any other member of this House, because he has inside information-was to seek a renewal of his mandate to Strengthen his arm, that he might carry on this war more effectively.
What would be the result now if this coercion measure is persisted in? You will

apply it, but how many recruits will you secure by it? Do you thiruc you can impose a measure of this kind upon an unwilling people who will not submit to it? We have evidence already that in some large cities in Canada there is no intention of submitting to coercion unless voted by the people in a constitutional manner.
I want Canada to continue her noble effort in this war. I think Canada has done splendidly ever since the war commenced. I think we have given evidences of our good-will in this matter of which we may well be proud, not only sending 400,000 men across the sea-np small contribution for a country of 7,000,000 of people-but assuming financial burdens so enormous that our children's children will hardly be able to pay them off. These things are greatly to the credit of the Canadian people. But why should not we remain united? Why should not Canadians from all provinces continue the effort so well begun? Why resort to coercive measures? Why not say to the people: our mandate has expired; we come hack to you, and if you have confidence in the Administration we will go back and continue Canada's participation in the war according to the means that our country can command.
The right hon. the Prime Minister said that as a Ne<w Year's gift he would authorize the raising of recruits to the number of 500,000 men. Hardly had the words fallen from his lips when one of the ablest men of Canada, Lord Shaughnessy, said that 500,000 .men could not be sent to the other side without seriously crippling our industries all over Canada. And those industries have been greatly affected as it is. We are told that we must maintain four divisions at the front 'The laws of the Medes and Persians alone could not he changed. Why must we maintain four divisions? Why not three, or five? I am not a military expert, and I question whether there are men in this House who are sufficiently qualified as military experts to say what is the particular value of four, pr three, or five divisions. Canada must continue to do what she can to help Britain and win the war. But we have been told over and over again that production in this country is necessary, that it cannot be dispensed with, that the man on the farm is as valuable in his way as the man in the trenches. Why not, before resorting to coercive methods, have a really competent tribunal, composed of men big enough to impress their views upon the country, tell us that Canada can raise so many men for military purposes, but must

retain so many men for production, and munition work? Are we to be told, on the mere say-so of the leader of one political party, that such and such a thing is to he done, and the whole country must submit?
The province of Quebec has objected to this Bill and will object to it because it has no faith in the present Government. For one thing half of the membership of the House from the province of Quebec has been elected to oppose the present Government and the other half from that province was elected in 1911 after the gospel had been preached that the citizens of Canada had no duty to fulfil to Britain outside of Canada in defence of her own territory. The result of that nefarious campaign in the province of Quebec was the bringing into power of the present Administration. The present Administration would never have occupied the treasury benches but for the men who were elected in Quebec under the resolutions adopted at the meeting at St. Eus-tache, and framed by Mr. Henri Bourassa and the late Mr. Monk. That was the platform upon which the colleagues, or allies, of the present Administration were elected in Quebec. We of the Liberal party, who stood loyally by the participation of Canada in British wars, who stood loyally in favour-of the creation of a Canadian navy, because we thought it our duty to do what we could for the defence of the Empire of which we are part and parcel, were condemned on every hustings in Quebec although Quebec stood loyally by us to the extent of half of its membership in. the House. To-day the views we preached are recognized by all parties in this province.
This afternoon I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). The minister went back to what happened in this House in the last three years and put to us the question: What we were going to do about it. Were we going to stop our efforts? Were we going to tell the men in the trenches that we were not going to send them any more assistance? My view of it is this: If you attempt coercion you will send less men to the trenches than if you appeal to the proper spirit of the people. Let us go now before the country. I am sure that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will consent to the adoption of the remaining Supply and we can have the verdict of the people in the next two months. If that verdict is in favour of coercive measures everybody will submit to
it. But if the verdict is in favour of carrying on the war as we have carried it on up to the present time, by appealing to the better sense, the better sentiment, of the Canadian people generally, we shall have the policy instituted and we will see that it is carried through.
I shall not, at this late hour, undertake to answer many of the points which were brought out because the House is pretty well informed upon all these things now. We have heard a great many allusions made to the province of Quebec and I do not want to say anything more particularly about that province. But, I will say that the people there are quite capable of coming to a decision 'and doing their duty properly. I am prepared to go back to my constituency, composed as it is of English and French-speaking Canadians, to meet the strongest representatives of the present Government that can be sent in joint debate before a French and English speaking audience, not only in my constituency but in any part of Quebec, and I am prepared to submit to the verdict of the people loyally no matter what that verdict is because in British governed countries when the people have spoken we must submit to their verdict. If the people of Canada think that coercive measures, that Germanized and Prussianized methods should prevail in Canada, and that they can do more for the allies than the methods of conciliation and union that we are preaching today, we shall submit to the verdict. But, I am satisfied that the people shall want first of all that Canada shall give the Allies a great example. What would be said tomorrow throughout the world if one-half of this country should chasten the other half and, by coercion bring about a contribution to the war when Great Britain is participating in this war on account of liberty and freedom?
We want to continue to do our full duty but we want to do it generously, we want to do it freely, we want to do it of our own free will, we want the man from Ontario to feel that his fellow Canadian citizen in the province of Quebec is prepared to defend his country, we want the people in the West to realize that if the Hun ever came to Canada it would be up the Saint-Lawrence river and that the citizens of Quebec would be the first to meet him. The citizens of Quebec have been called upon to meet the invader before. They met the invader in 1776, they repelled him from before the fortress of Quebec and forever after the British flag was kept flying over the citadel. They met the

invader on the banks of the Cha-*teauguay in 1812 and on that occasion de Salaberry and his 300 men were able to turn 7,000 Americans back to their own lines. In the present war the handful of French Canadians, 14,000 or 15,000 in number, who have enlisted in Quebec have shown at Langemarck, at Saint-Julien, at Ypres, and at Courcelette, that they are worthy descendants of the pioneers of Quebec. We want to do our share and that i3 why we do not want to be tabooed, we do not want to be ostracized, because after all the French race are the oldest Canadian settlers. This is our native soil and this is the flag that we accepted freely when the other was returned to the country from which it came. We of the province of Quebec are the oldest inhabitants of this territory. Quebec remains as it was at the time of Confederation, the keystone of the aroh. Without the free consent of the province of Quebec there would not have been any Confederation and the Prime Minister in quoting the words of the Militia Act repeated several times the name of Sir George Etienne Cartier. You will find such names as George Etienne Cartier and Louis Hippolyte La Fontaine at every step in the constitutional history of Canada. The corner stone of free, constitutional government in Canada was laid by the broad manhood of the British stock of Ontario and the Frenchmen of the province of Quebec who accepted the new duties imposed upon them as subjects of the King were loyal to the country.
But three or four days ago the Governor General of Canada accepted an address in the city of Quebec from the Mayor and the Premier of the province and was given assurance that the province of Quebec remained still the old Loyalist province of the Dominion. Is it because you fall short of a few thousand men that you are going to ostracize these people? Is it because after 150 years of faithful service to the British flag you are going to tear asunder the bond of friendship that exist between the French and English in this country?
I do not think that after mature deliberation it will be found to be the intention of the present Government to do so. We have the evidence of the Prime Minister who was willing, if the leader of the Opposition entered a coalition, to pass the measure and then submit it to the people. That was the intention of the Government. Why not do it now? If you have a majority and you pass the measure, it will be 
a slim majority. Suppose you have 25, 15 or 10 of a majority, is that a mandate to impose such a coercive measure as this which will deprive any citizen of Canada of his personal liberty? Do you consider that you have a mandate in the seventh session of the twelfth Parliament* when the constitution of the country says that five years shall be the terrp of Parliament, when you have 20 seats or more vacant, when the western provinces are not represented as they should be and when we have been elected on a franchise framed on the census of 1901 which is 16 years old? We have here twenty seats that are not represented. I receive letters daily from Kestigouche, in New Brunswick, which adjoins my own riding; people write me saying: Our member has been dead for four years, we are not represented at Ottawa, will you kindly attend to this and to that? I do so cheerfully. Is that the kind of Parliament that should undertake to impose such a measure as this upon the people? I say no, Mr. Speaker. The Premier of Canada comes from a province where British principles are better understood than this. He comes from the old province of Nova Scotia, which was the first North American province to adopt responsible government. He understands what the British principle is, that to give force and strength to a measure you must have public approval, and you must have the consent of the people, the consent of the governed.
I say this, and these are my last words, we in this Chamber, no matter what our origin is, no matter what language we speak, whether we speak one or two or three languages, we are all citizens of Canada, we are all British subjects, we are friends, devotees of the Allies, admirers of the great principles for which they are contending; and I would be unworthy of my origin, and every member of this House would be unworthy of his, if he fell back at the present moment. But when there is such a serious difference of opinion on this point, I think that there is ample justification for sending this measure to the people. We should have another general election, we should explain to the people the position as it is now, we should make them understand exactly what has been done and what remains to be done, and I have faith in the verdict of the people; I have faith that there is still enough patriotism left, not only in my own province but in every province of Canada, to send back to this House a body of men who will be deter-

mined to uphold our institutions, because we know that the defeat of Britain and her Allies in this war would mean the wiping out of our free institutions in North America. We differ only as to method. I appeal to the majority of this House, I appeal to the majority who come from Ontario and from the western provinces as well, to delay this measure, not to go too fast with it, because they may do more harm than good. I am not in favour of the slacker, I am not in favour of protecting the man who should do his duty, but I want a mandate to do that; I want to go back to my people, and when I get that mandate I will come back and I will legislate in this 'House any measure that is called for by the circumstances. . But at the present time I have no such mandate, and for those reasons I shall vote for the amendment offered by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and against the second reading of the Bill, regretting to do so, because I would have liked, for the name and for the honour of Canada, that we should have continued our participation in the war unanimously, both parties agreeing to all our w.ar measures as in the past. But if necessity compels me to vote against the Bill I shall do so. I shall do so, not because I am opposed to conscription as >an anti-democratic measure, but because I have no mandate from my people, and because I want to serve the cause of the Allies by clearing up the situation and coming back with a mandate before imposing such a measure.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman appeals to the House for a dissolution and a general election, as he desires a mandate. He states that he is not opposed to conscription. In the event of such a dissolution, would he appeal for a mandate for conscription or against conscription?

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: I would go back to the people and explain the position exactly as I found it and knew it, and if the people favoured conscription I would come back here and support it.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: What would you yourself ask for?

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: If you would supply me with the information that the Prime Minister of this country has I could give you my answer, but until I get that information I am iasked to vote in the dark, and, therefore, I cannot do so.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
You do not know
whether you are against it or for it?

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext: I am not against conscription, per se, or because I think it an antidemocratic measure, but if it had any worth in it it should have been adopted in 1914, and the Liberal party should have been called in then to join hands with our friends so that we could have had a united effort. But we did not insist on that; we supported you just the same.

subsubtopic: THE SECOND READING OF THE BILL MOVED.
speechtext:
It would not have been tyranny or coercion then?
On the motion of Mr. Morrikon, the debate was adjourned.
